# Bounded count-free Weisfeiler–Leman dimension for uniquely decomposable groups

**Theorem.** Fix a positive integer $d$. Each finite group with a unique fully refined internal direct product decomposition into factors generated by at most $d$ elements has count-free Weisfeiler–Leman dimension bounded in terms of $d$. The comparison group can be arbitrary. Uniqueness refers to the set of actual subgroups in a fully refined decomposition. This answers Question 7.1 of Johnson, Levet, Vojtěchovský and Widholm. [Original question](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.06478v3#S7)

The group-division test from the companion logspace proof yields a bounded-variable formula for direct-factorhood of a subgroup given by a bounded number of generators. The unique factors can then be defined in the group, and strict chains of coordinate supports recover their multiplicities.

## 1. Fixed-variable formulas for group operations

Use first-order logic with equality and the ternary multiplication relation. To compare two finite groups, fix $N$ at least the order of either. The sentence may depend on $N$ and the pair. The variable bound will be independent of $N$ and of the number of factors.

A fixed word equation uses a constant number of extra variable names beyond its free variables. Evaluate a product by splitting it into two subproducts and using reusable endpoint and midpoint names. Unbounded conjunctions or disjunctions here mean finite formulas of unconstrained length on the fixed pair. In particular, membership in the subgroup generated by a $d$-tuple is a disjunction of word tests of length at most $N$, since a shortest path in a Cayley graph never repeats vertices.

More generally, if $R(s)$ defines a set of possible generators with a bounded number of free parameters, test a step from $u$ to $v$ by requiring $v=us$ with $R(s)$ or $R(s^{-1})$. A bounded-variable formula tests for a path with at most $N$ such steps, combining paths by midpoint quantification with three reusable endpoint names. Allowing stationary steps permits rounding the length bound up to a power of two. A step formula reserves separate scratch names and retains the original parameters. The elements reachable from the identity are exactly the subgroup generated by $R$ in either comparison group. Thus taking the subgroup generated by a definable set adds only a constant number of variable names. The balanced constructions for a word or path of length at most $N$ have quantifier depth $O(\log N)$ beyond the depth of the step test.

## 2. Define when a boundedly generated subgroup splits off

For a length-$d$ tuple $\bar a$, let $P=\langle\bar a\rangle$ and let $C=C_X(P)$ in the ambient group $X$. Membership in $P$ is as above. Membership in $C$ requires commutation with the entries of $\bar a$. The condition $X=PC$ is a quantified product test. Put $D=P\cap C$. Then $D$ is central in $C$. Under $X=PC$, the subgroup $P$ has a direct complement in $X$ exactly when $D$ has a direct complement in $C$. Indeed $X=P\times B$ implies $C=Z(P)\times B$. Conversely, $C=D\times B$ gives $X=PB$ with commuting factors and trivial intersection.

Since $D$ is central in $C$, it splits exactly when the natural map $j:D\to B_0=C/[C,C]$ is injective and has direct-summand image. Abelianize a split product for necessity. For sufficiency take the inverse image of a complementary subgroup of $B_0$.

For a finite abelian group $B$, write $W_{p,k}(B)=B[p]\cap p^{k-1}B$ additively. The condition on $j$ is equivalent to injectivity of all the induced maps
$$
W_{p,k}(D)/W_{p,k+1}(D)\longrightarrow W_{p,k}(B_0)/W_{p,k+1}(B_0).
$$
A split inclusion gives injectivity in every grade. Conversely, choose a cyclic prime-power basis of $D$. Independence in the grades allows the images of its length-$k$ cyclic factors' bottom elements to be extended to bases in the corresponding grades of $B_0$. For the prescribed bottom vectors use the images of the source cyclic generators as lifts. Pick any lifts of the added bottom vectors. They give a cyclic basis of $B_0$: their bottom vectors form a basis of the primary torsion, so the map from the product of their abstract cyclic groups has trivial kernel. A nonzero kernel would contain an element of prime order. The product of the cyclic orders equals the order of $B_0$ by the cyclic classification and its grade dimensions. This proves the splitting criterion.

One grade's injectivity can be expressed directly. For every $w\in D$ with $w^p=1$ that is a $p^{k-1}$-st power in $D$, require that if
$$
\exists c\in C\quad c^{p^k}w^{-1}\in[C,C],
$$
then $w$ is a $p^k$-th power in $D$. The torsion condition ensures that the image of $w$ is already in $B_0[p]$. Membership in $[C,C]$ uses Section 1 with the generator predicate for commutators of pairs in $C$. Take the finite conjunction over all primes and positive grades with $p^k\le N$, since all higher source grades are zero. This gives exactly direct-factorhood, with only a constant number of additional variables beyond $\bar a$.

## 3. Define the factors and certify the product

Fix the reference group $G$ in the stated class. Let $T$ range over the isomorphism types of its nontrivial indecomposable factors. For each $T$, fix one generating $d$-tuple, padded by identities if needed, and one word for each element of $T$. A marked-table formula in $\bar a$ asserts that the word values are distinct, multiply according to the table of $T$, and evaluate to the entries of $\bar a$ on the marked generators. This is a conjunction of fixed-word tests. The word values form a subgroup containing the tuple, all of whose values lie in its generated subgroup. Thus it tests exactly whether the marking extends to an isomorphism $T\to\langle\bar a\rangle$.

A candidate of type $T$ is a tuple satisfying both the marked-table test and direct-factorhood. Use the finite disjunction over reference types to define candidates of any type. In $G$ they represent precisely the indecomposable factors of the unique decomposition. Indeed any candidate is directly indecomposable, and refining a complement includes it in a fully refined decomposition. Conversely every factor has a marking. Equality of the subgroups represented by two tuples is expressible by mutual membership of their generators, with two length-$d$ tuples.

For a candidate subgroup $P$, define $K(P)$ to be the subgroup generated by all the other candidate subgroups. Membership is a bounded-variable test by Section 1: in the generator predicate quantify a second candidate tuple whose subgroup differs from $P$. The same method defines the subgroup generated by all candidates. Assert both of the following.

- The candidate subgroups generate all of $X$.
- Each candidate subgroup $P$ commutes with $K(P)$ and intersects $K(P)$ trivially.

These conditions hold in $G$. In any comparison group satisfying them, multiply one element from each distinct candidate subgroup. The resulting map from the product is a surjective homomorphism by the commutation and generation conditions. A tuple in its kernel has each coordinate in its own factor and in the product of the others, hence each is the identity. The multiplication map is therefore an isomorphism. The comparison group need not be assumed to have a unique decomposition.

## 4. Express multiplicity by inclusion chains

In a certified product, $x\in K(P)$ exactly when the $P$-coordinate of $x$ is the identity. Let the type-$T$ support of $x$ be the set of type-$T$ candidate subgroups at which its coordinate is nonidentity. The support of $x$ is contained in that of $y$ precisely when $y\in K(P)$ implies $x\in K(P)$ for every candidate tuple of type $T$. The strict relation adds the negation of reverse inclusion. Every subset of the type-$T$ factors is realized as a support, by coordinate independence and the fact that factors are nontrivial. Therefore the maximum number of strict edges in a chain is the number of type-$T$ factors.

A chain of any externally fixed length can be expressed by repeatedly quantifying a next element in the strict-inclusion relation. This reuses two chain endpoint names and the scratch names for the relation. For each reference type with multiplicity $m_T$, assert a chain of length $m_T$ and exclude a chain of length $m_T+1$. The comparison sentence now forces the same product of factor types as $G$, hence isomorphism. If the reference group is trivial, the generation condition for the empty set of candidates says exactly that $X$ is trivial.

Every formula uses $O(d)$ variable names. A generated-subgroup construction adds a bounded number of names to its generator predicate, and their nesting depth is fixed. The number of conjuncts, lengths of words and number of chain links affect the formula length or quantifier depth, while all reuse the same names. By the corresponding count-free pebble game on the ternary multiplication relation, the distinguishing sentences yield bounded count-free Weisfeiler–Leman dimension in Version I. Version II has a stronger initial test: the marked subgroup records all the atomic multiplication information used by Version I. Its count-free refinement preserves this dominance. Thus bounded dimension also holds in Version II. [WL definitions and pebble games](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.06478v3#S2)

For equal-order groups of order $n$, take $N=n$. The marked words can have length at most $n$, and the formulas use balanced words, powers and reachability with fixed nesting. The chain tests have at most $\log_2 n+1$ links in the formula, since the reference decomposition has at most $\log_2 n$ factors. The quantifier depth is therefore $O(\log n)$ and gives that round bound. This is an informal proof.

## 5. A logarithmic-logarithmic round bound in Version II

The same class is identified with $O(\log\log n)$ rounds of count-free Version II. This uses the bounded-width lemma of the companion [constant-round counting proof](ConstantRoundCountingWL.md): if $X$ is a product of $d$-generated groups and $X=PC_X(P)$, then every element of $[C_X(P),C_X(P)]$ is a product of $b(d)$ commutators in $C_X(P)$. To recall its proof, project to each factor $Q_i$. Then $Q_i=P_iC_{Q_i}(P_i)$ and $C_{Q_i}(P_i)/Z(P_i)$ is a quotient of $Q_i$ and hence $d$-generated. Lifting these generators generates the centralizer up to a central subgroup. Its derived subgroup is exactly that of the subgroup on the lifts. Apply the Nikolov–Segal commutator-width theorem to each lift subgroup and combine the commutator expressions coordinatewise. [Nikolov–Segal](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2007/165-1/p05)

For Version II, every fixed word equation on the variables in use is an atomic test on their marked subgroup. In particular, powers with arbitrarily large fixed exponents, membership in a subgroup generated by a fixed tuple using a disjunction over words, and the known marked-table tests are available without adding quantifier depth. Use the constant-depth predicate for a product of $b(d)$ commutators in $C_X(P)$, padding with identities. In the sentence, require that whenever $X=PC_X(P)$ for a candidate marking passing the type test, this bounded product set is closed under multiplication. It already contains all commutators, contains the identity, and is closed under inverses. Closure makes it exactly the derived subgroup. The guard holds in the reference group and ensures exactness in any comparison group satisfying the sentence. Now the direct-factor test of Section 2 has constant quantifier depth.

We also have a constant-depth formula testing whether $x$ belongs to some complement to a candidate $P$. First require $x\in C=C_X(P)$. Set $D=Z(P)$ and let $\bar x$ be the image of $x$ in $C_{\rm ab}$. The remaining condition is that the map
$$
D\longrightarrow C_{\rm ab}/\langle\bar x\rangle
$$
be injective with direct-summand image. Indeed a splitting gives a retraction from that quotient onto $D$, whose composite with $C$ kills $x$. The kernel is then a complement to $D$ in $C$ and to $P$ in $X$. Conversely any complement to $P$ containing $x$ yields that retraction. Use the same grade-injectivity test as in Section 2. Membership of $c^{p^k}w^{-1}$ in the inverse image of $\langle\bar x\rangle$ is the disjunction that $c^{p^k}w^{-1}x^{-a}$ belongs to $[C,C]$ for an integer $0\le a<N$. This adds no quantifier depth, since all word equations are atomic and $N$ is at least the order of the group.

Write $K(P)$ for the set defined by this complement-membership formula. In $G$ it is the unique complement, since any complement refines into exactly the other actual factors. Replace the product certification in Section 3 by the constant-depth assertions that every $K(P)$ is a subgroup and a direct complement to $P$, that every different candidate $Q$ is contained in $K(P)$, and that $\bigcap_P K(P)=1$. These are quantified checks using the same fixed number of tuple and element variables. The assertions hold in $G$. In any other model of the sentence, form the simultaneous projections to all distinct candidate subgroups using the certified complements. The kernel is their intersection and thus trivial. Since each candidate is in every other complement, the image contains all coordinate axes of the target product, so it is surjective. This certifies the product with the same interpretation of coordinate supports as before.

Finally, express a strict support chain of length $\ell$ between two endpoints by splitting it into lengths $\lfloor\ell/2\rfloor$ and $\lceil\ell/2\rceil$ and quantifying over their common midpoint. This needs three reusable endpoint names and depth $O(\log(\ell+1))$ beyond the base strict inclusion test. Every multiplicity test uses $\ell\le \log_2 n+1$. Word equations are preserved by every legal partial correspondence in the Version II game. Thus the bounded-variable formula argument in this enriched vocabulary gives the asserted $O(\log\log n)$ rounds for equal-order comparisons. Different orders are distinguished immediately under the game's convention.
